claims.text: Protective oxide formation and retention in multicomponent HEAs is governed by inherently sluggish diffusion.
The relevant diffusion balance selectively promotes outward migration of Al and Cr while retarding inward oxygen transport.
This diffusion balance produces a thin, dense, and adherent Al2O3, Cr2O3, or mixed-oxide scale.
An Al2O3- or Cr2O3-based scale acts as a barrier that retards further oxidation.
The intended HEA contains approximately 10–20 at.% of one or more strong oxide formers such as Al or Cr.
The initial AlCrFeCoNi-type alloy is a homogeneous or metastable solid solution.
Exposure in air or an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 900–1100 °C for roughly 48–100 hours is suitable for developing and evaluating the oxide scale.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous, compact, and adherent surface scale primarily containing Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3.
The microstructural development of the protective scale is mediated by sluggish diffusion in the complex HEA matrix.
Large configurational entropy and lattice distortion in HEAs slow the diffusion of both metal cations and oxygen.
Slow transport kinetics enhance selective outward Al and Cr transport and their preferential surface oxidation.
Limited oxygen ingress and cation mobility prevent rapid oxide buildup and spallation.
An HEA with higher Al/Cr content will have lower oxidation mass gain than a similar HEA with lower Al/Cr content.
The higher-Al/Cr HEA will develop a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale than the lower-Al/Cr baseline.
Alloys with lower concentrations of strong oxide formers typically form thicker, non-protective, or non-adherent scales.
The proposed mechanism applies to HEAs or refractory complex concentrated alloys containing at least one passivating element, Al or Cr, in oxygen-rich environments at 900–1100 °C.
High Mn content can dominate oxidation by producing non-protective Mn-rich oxides.
The quantitative effects of multielement interactions, thermal cycling on adhesion, and minor alloying additions remain uncertain.
A controlled comparison can vary Al/Cr content while holding oxidation temperature, time, atmosphere, and other parameters constant, then measure mass gain and scale structure.
Failure of the higher-Al/Cr alloy to show lower mass gain and/or a continuous, compact, adherent scale is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
